articles.text:
A simple explainer of the massive crypto heist at Binance : NPR
Accessibility links
Skip to main content
Keyboard shortcuts for audio player
A simple explainer of the massive crypto heist at Binance Here are five things to know about the massive hack of the crypto exchange Binance — from how it happened to what it means for the sector.
Business
A simple explainer of the massive $6.3 billion crypto heist at Binance
October 31, 20262:11 PM ET
By
Rafael Nam
A North Korean hacking unit is widely believed to be behind the $6.3 billion cyber heist of crypto exchange Binance.
Justin Sullivan/Getty Images North America
hide caption
Justin Sullivan/Getty Images North America
It was the biggest cyber heist in history.
Business
A Trump-backed crypto bill just suffered a bruising defeat in the Senate. Here's why
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchanges, was hacked this week, with cybercriminals plundering more than $6 billion. Experts widely believe the hackers were a sophisticated unit within the North Korean military that has a track record of committing cyber heists.
The theft stunned the crypto industry and set off new fears about a sector that many critics deride as the "Wild West" of finance.
Here are 5 things to know about the spectacular heist.
So first, what are crypto exchanges?
They are akin to the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) or the Nasdaq, but instead of trading stocks, investors turn to Binance and other crypto exchanges to trade digital assets such as Bitcoin.
A wide range of investors trade cryptocurrencies at these exchanges, from financial institutions and sophisticated traders, all the way to regular investors looking to make some money.
OK, so what happened this week?
At 4:05 p.m. Eastern on Thursday, hackers were able to access the accounts of investors who trade cryptocurrencies at Binance. It took only about 20 minutes for these hackers to make off off with just over $6.3 billion worth of cryptocurrencies.
Technology
Hacking attempts rise after flaws found in program affecting 70% of websites
Ari Redbord, the global head of policy at TRM Labs, a crypto research firm that has helped Binance trace and recover some of the stolen funds, calls it "the largest bank robbery in human history."
"Imagine a world where someone could walk into a bank and walk out with $6.36 billion in stolen funds and then move those funds at the speed of the internet," he says. "This is bank robbery in the age of technology."
But a lot of details about the heist are still unclear, including how exactly the hackers were able to hack their way into the trading accounts of investors at Binance.
Binance, working with other exchanges and partners, has been able to freeze about $3 billion in stolen cryptocurrencies, effectively preventing hackers from taking full possession of its digital assets.
The exchange has also said it will pay back any customers who were victims of the cyber heist — though it's not clear exactly how it will do that.
Why do experts believe it's North Korea?
The level of sophistication and speed of the hack all point to a North Korean military hacking unit widely known as TraderTraitor. The unit was also responsible for what was the previous biggest-ever cyber heist, the theft of $1.5 billion from crypto exchange Bybit last year.
"North Korea has built the most sophisticated cyber capabilities in the world. They have a cadre of teams of professional hackers who are part of their military," says TRM's Redbord.
"This isn't just a commercial hacker who's looking to make some money," he adds. "This is going to be used for weapons proliferation and other destabilizing activity."
Experts say North Korean hackers are very sophisticated and motivated. Pictured are Korean People's Army soldiers bowing before the statues of late North Korean leaders Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il on the 32nd anniversary of Kim Il Sung's death, at Mansu Hill in Pyongyang on July 8, 2026.
Kim Won Jin/AFP via Getty Images
hide caption
Kim Won Jin/AFP via Getty Images
What does this heist tell us about the safety of crypto exchanges?
Researchers say it's too early to determine whether there were any major flaws with Binance's security systems. But they say the heist is a clear sign of just how sophisticated North Korean hackers are.
Meanwhile, crypto critics say the way Binance and other crypto exchanges are set up deserve scrutiny.
National Security
FBI hunting the hackers who stole its employees' sensitive data
A unique feature of crypto exchanges is that people can buy and sell digital currencies such as bitcoin — and leave them with the exchanges for safekeeping.
This dual trust in the exchange makes them mighty tempting targets for hackers. And what's more concerning for critics, crypto exchanges also don't have to follow the same strict regulations that govern established Wall Street firm.
"You may trade on the New York Stock Exchange, but you don't keep your funds with the New York Stock Exchange. You keep it with your broker — and your broker is audited and regulated by the SEC (Securities and Exchange Commission)," says Amanda Fischer, policy director and chief operating officer at financial consumer advocacy group Better Markets. "And your broker has to pay for insurance that will make customers whole in the event that there's a cyber attack."
"So the regulatory framework for crypto is much weaker than what investors in the US enjoy in other markets," says Fischer.
Though Binance has promised to pay back customers who lost funds, it is not necessarily bound to do so according to current regulations. And many critics worry that smaller exchanges could struggle to pay back their investors in case of a hack, leaving these traders to suffer the consequences.
Doesn't this reinforce the crypto sector's Wild West reputation?
For many crypto critics, it does. They warn the lack of clear regulations for crypto executives could lead to perverse incentives at these exchanges.

West Virginia and data centers: State faces new extractive industry Residents are fighting back against plans for a project that would span thousands of acres near the Monongahela National Forest and popular outdoor recreation, ski areas and dark sky sites.
National
Plans for a data center threaten scenic wilderness and dark skies in West Virginia
October 31, 20265:00 AM ET
By
Scott Neuman
White Grass Ski Touring Center in Canaan Valley , W.Va., is celebrated for its unusually curvy and hilly cross-country skiing terrain.
Chris Jackson for NPR
hide caption
Chris Jackson for NPR
DAVIS, W.Va. — Stretching nearly a million acres through the rugged mountains of eastern West Virginia, the Monongahela National Forest links some of the state's best known natural attractions. The vast area ranges from the ski slopes of Canaan Valley to the dark skies of Blackwater Falls and Spruce Knob and includes the small towns of Davis and Thomas that serve as gateways for visitors to the region.
Climate
Data centers are booming. But there are big energy and environmental risks
For the past seven months, Kaleb Skelton, his wife, Ella, their 2-year-old son, Ryder, and dog Mabel have lived in a camper in this corner of West Virginia's "almost heaven." Kaleb is finishing a seasonal stint as a campground manager on a lake near Spruce Knob, the state's highest point.
On clear nights atop the isolated peak, they get to experience a river of stars in one of the very few pockets of darkness remaining in the Eastern United States. The area has become a draw for amateur astronomers.
Spruce Knob Lake Campground hosts Kaleb and Ella Skelton, at their site at Spruce Knob on Saturday, Oct. 10 2026 in Spruce Knob, W.Va. The couple from Texas have been at the site since April and said they have never seen darker skies than atop Spruce Knob.
Chris Jackson for NPR
hide caption
Chris Jackson for NPR
During summer's new moons, Kaleb says, one in four campsites he oversees is occupied by someone with a telescope. He thought his family's cabin in eastern Texas offered "the craziest" dark skies he'd ever seen, "but coming out here definitely rivals it."
A dark history for 'Stump Town'
Those inky-black nights — and the natural beauty they shelter — are now under threat from what many residents see as a modern-day version of extractive industries like logging and mining that once defined the region. In a place where tourism, outdoor recreation and community are deeply intertwined, a gigantic power plant and data center campus in nearby Tucker County would bring large-scale development into the heart of it all.
A stark image of the town of Davis from 1885, during the heyday of logging, is a reminder of that transformation. The photo shows a handful of squat buildings amid a broad clearing littered with forest remains.
They used to call it "Stump Town," says Kim Williams, president of the Snow Sports Museum of West Virginia in Canaan Valley. At the turn of the century, massive first-growth trees dominated the landscape.
Then, logging companies "came in and clear-cut the whole valley and everything around it," he says.
National
West Virginia paid digital nomads to move there during COVID. Many are staying
By the early 20th century, entire mountainsides of red spruce and eastern hemlock had been stripped bare. Then came the coal companies, which left the nearby Blackwater River acidic and dangerous to drink.
Today, the scars still show. The big trees won't return for generations, but a century of natural regrowth, conservation and deliberate restoration means the land is on its way to healing.
While few expect that the latest tech boom presages anything like the environmental destruction of the past, many see the proposed new Ridgeline data center as a big step backward, undoing the progress the local community has made to recover.
A roughly 785-megawatt generating plant is slated to be the first part of "a large-scale data and energy infrastructure project designed to support artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and enterprise systems," according to Purcellville, Va.-based Fundamental Data LLC, the company behind Ridgeline.
The photo "The Birth of a city, Davis, W. Va. in 1885" by William Henry Jackson shows a handful of squat buildings amid a broad clearing littered with forest remains.
hide caption
The complex would rely primarily on natural gas, with diesel as a backup fuel source. Power generated on-site, rather than purchased from the regional grid, could ease some concerns about the project's effects on electricity rates. It does not, however, resolve concerns over air and water pollution.
Located on a reclaimed coal-mining site, plans are for an initial 291 acres that could eventually expand to 10,000 acres — 15 square miles — and include parts of neighboring Grant County, according to local news reports.
Speaking to NPR, Casey Chapman, listed in court documents as Fundamental Data's "responsible individual," declined to speculate on the facility's ultimate size, saying only that "if fully developed … it would be thousands of acres."
Only on NPR
The data center backlash is reshaping American politics — one community at a time
Light pollution is a common complaint from residents living near data centers. Chapman says the company will use "well-designed" lighting to help minimize the effects of sky glow, in an effort not to jeopardize nearby Blackwater Falls State Park's pursuit of an official dark-sky certification.
An analysis by the Northern Virginia Astronomy Club, which hosts an annual star party in the region, found that Ridgeline's initial footprint could increase sky glow near Blackwater by 528%, transforming its nighttime rural sky to one comparable to a suburban area. (The same analysis found only a minimal impact on Spruce Knob.)

Oil company earnings skyrocket — again Oil companies are reporting another quarter of sky-high profits as the war in Iran pushes up the price of oil — and prices at the pump.
Business
Oil company earnings skyrocket — again
October 31, 20265:00 AM ET
Heard on Weekend Edition Saturday
Willa Rubin
Pump prices stay high as big oil reports sky-high profits
Listen
4:19
4:19
Transcript
Download
Embed
<iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6008072/nx-s1-9986689" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Transcript
A pump jack operates at sunset in the Permian Basin near Loving, N.M., on Tuesday, May 20, 2025.
Susan Montoya Bryan/AP
hide caption
Susan Montoya Bryan/AP
Sign up for the Planet Money newsletter. The world is confusing. Economics can help.
Oil companies made billions this quarter, they told investors on calls this week. ExxonMobil earned $15.4 billion, more than doubling its earnings compared to this time last year.
Shell nearly doubled its own earnings, at $10.8 billion.
Chevron's were up 180%, at $9.9 billion.
Together, the three companies pulled in just over $36 billion this quarter.
Middle East conflict
Oil companies report sky-high profits thanks to wartime crude prices
As with the soaring profits oil companies recorded last quarter, it's largely due to the war in Iran disrupting the global oil supply. Less oil is moving through the Middle East, so the oil in other parts of the world has become much more valuable.
Brent crude is now trading around $113 a barrel. For context, before the war began, it was about $70 a barrel.
Business
Tariffs, diesel and computer chips are driving up costs for automakers
Business
The Trump administration weakens fuel efficiency standards for new cars
Meanwhile, demand for oil and refined products like gasoline, diesel and heating oil hasn't changed much. People still need them to heat homes, drive cars, run tractors and truck everything we buy around the country.
Dan Pickering, founder of the financial services firm Pickering Energy Partners, says that big oil companies are profiting as they meet that demand. " The majors are able to sell their barrels that they produce in the U.S. or Latin America or Europe for much higher prices," he said. "So the Middle East's loss is generally the gain of oil and gas companies in the U.S. and Europe."
On their earnings calls, oil company executives said a good chunk of their profits were going to their shareholders through dividends and stock buybacks. Shell's buyback was one of their biggest ever. Exxon announced its highest-ever quarterly dividend.
But for the most part, Pickering says, these companies are in a wait-and-see stance — they're not really spending that money on things like new drilling projects, because they know they're in an unusual moment.
"This is a period where the high prices are driven more by geopolitical events than anything else," he said. Since it's hard to predict how long those will last, he continued, "You put the money in the bank and watch to see what happens as we move into 2027."
Pickering says this makes sense because oil is a cyclical industry — prices move up and down. Companies want to hold onto their cash when times are good so they can insulate themselves when they're not so good.
A supply shock, amid two ongoing wars
The rising cost of oil has pushed up what drivers pay at the pump. Gasoline now costs about $1.20 more per gallon than it did a year ago, according to AAA. Diesel hit a record high in September, and is still close to that high.
Exxon CEO Darren Woods was one of the few to directly address the issue on an earnings call, saying, "We recognize the impact high prices have on people's lives and economic growth."
Exxon's solution, he said, is to boost production. " With products in short supply, our teams have done everything they can to keep prices down by maximizing production," he said.
Chevron CEO Mike Wirth made a similar point, telling investors, " What we can do is what we can control, and that's help consumers get as much as they possibly can out of our systems."
On these calls, executives from all the companies pointed out that they're dealing with a massive supply shock. The war in Iran, as well as Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries, have taken a lot of global refining capacity offline.
The executives indicated that they don't see the situation changing anytime soon.
"If you'd asked me six months ago, would I have thought that oil prices were going to be where they are today — no," Shell CEO Wael Sawan said on his company's call. "Personally, I thought we were at a high there, and we were essentially looking at what was going to be a temporal spike."
Business
The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve is low. Here's why you should care
But because the war has gone on this long, global oil reserves are at much lower levels. The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve is at low levels; Europe released some of its crude oil and diesel.
"We're now seeing more and more structural stability in that higher oil price simply because we are seeing that inventory levels are being drawn down very quickly, and it's going to take quite some time to be able to refill that inventory," Sawan continued.
Calls for a windfall tax
Democrats in both chambers of Congress have called for a tax on windfall profits — excess profits that come about because of geopolitical forces outside of their control, not because of innovation. Bills introduced this spring would return some of those profits to Americans through tax rebates.
Climate
Oil companies are making billions. In the U.S., calls to tax their windfall are growing
Earlier this year, Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), who sponsored a windfall tax bill in the Senate, said he hopes it will also spotlight how climate-friendly renewable energy is incr

The French protests are clashing with the reality of France’s enormous debt : Planet Money In recent months, there have been serious whispers about an outrageous possibility: that one day soon, France — the seventh largest economy in the world — might not be able to pay back its debts. Right now, protesters in France are complaining about crumbling schools, the lack of teachers, and the overall high cost of living. But the government is struggling to find the money to address all the country’s problems.
France is in a lot of debt. It has been borrowing record amounts of money. So have many other countries including the U.S., the U.K., Italy, Canada. For more than a decade, there has been an international borrowing spree going on. Now, as interest rates climb, that borrowing spree might have to come to an end. And the consequences could get ugly.

articles.title: Blockchain intelligence firms link North Korea to $6.3B hack on Binance
articles.text:
Blockchain intelligence firms link North Korea to $6.3B hack on Binance : NPR
Accessibility links
Skip to main content
Keyboard shortcuts for audio player
Blockchain intelligence firms link North Korea to $6.3B hack on Binance The world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange reported Thursday that approximately $6.3 billion was impacted in an apparent hack.
Asia
Blockchain intelligence firms link North Korea to $6.3B hack on Binance
October 30, 20269:01 AM ET
By
The Associated Press
FILE - The Binance logo is seen on a smartphone, Feb. 28, 2023, in Marple Township, Pa.
Matt Slocum/AP
hide caption
Matt Slocum/AP
A U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm says a North Korean unit was likely behind the hack that impacted more than $6 billion on Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange.
Binance said it worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets. It said Friday that it was beginning to recover assets for users.
The cryptocurrency exchange said deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals have been suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two. It said it will cover all losses.
The company said on X that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, but that a subsequent investigation uncovered additional "points of breach."
TRM, in a post on its website Thursday, attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea's elite hacking unit. "We make this judgment with high confidence," the firm said.
"An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," TRM said. That would make the hack the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, it said.
In February last year, another cryptocurrency exchange, Bybit, suffered a $1.5 billion hit when it was hacked. The FBI said North Korea and TraderTraitor were responsible for the hack.
"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack," TRM said.
Blockchain analysis company Chainalysis also believed the Binance hack was "likely done by DPRK group TraderTraitor," its co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin wrote on X. DPRK stands for the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, North Korea's official name.
Asked about the potential ties to North Korea, a Binance spokesperson said only that the company is "working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice."
Experts say North Korea has turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.
In December 2022, South Korea's spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets in the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea's capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the best in the world.
Changpeng Zhao, also known as CZ, founded Binance in 2017. In 2023, he pleaded guilty to a felony linked to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform, and stepped down as the company's CEO. U.S. President Donald Trump pardoned Zhao in 2025.
Zhao posted Thursday on X that "User funds are safe!" but added that the theft "does look like a hack on Binance." He added that while he doesn't manage Binance anymore, "as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."
The event, meanwhile, also raises questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, cofounder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab.
"This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet.
Binance said on X it had "found no evidence of any wallet private key leak" and that the company would release more technical details when its probe is complete.

Binance flags 'potential security issue,' says approximately $6.3 billion impacted
October 30, 20267:21 AM ET
By
The Associated Press
FILE - The Binance logo is seen on a smartphone, Feb. 28, 2023, in Marple Township, Pa.
Matt Slocum/AP
hide caption
Matt Slocum/AP
LOS ANGELES — Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said Thursday it's investigating reports of a potential security issue as its founder said the incident "does look like a hack on Binance." The company said late Thursday the estimated total impact was at more than $6 billion, which could be one of the most significant of such security incidents on record.
Business
Crypto soared in 2025 — and then crashed. Now what?
It wasn't immediately clear the extent of the damage hackers might have been able to cause, and Binance had not explicitly confirmed that funds had been pilfered. The company said its teams are "working around the clock" to resolve the issue.
"Rest assured that user funds are completely safe," a Binance spokesperson said in a statement.
"Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information," the statement continued.
The company wrote on its X account that the estimated total impact sat at around $6.3 billion. It said it has worked with blockchain partners to freeze affected assets, with roughly $3 billion frozen on-chain so far.
"Binance's initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions," the company wrote.
"We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak," it added.
Binance said it will share more technical details once the investigation is complete and when the facts are "fully verified."
"Our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets," the company wrote in a separate post earlier Thursday.
Binance also said all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while it conducts security checks, freezes funds and works with law enforcement.
Stablecoin providers Tether and Circle each said they froze funds Thursday in response to the incident.
Jeremy Allaire, co-founder and CEO of Circle, wrote on X that the company had frozen the equivalent of more than $800 million in currency associated with the incident "in coordination with law enforcement." Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said on X that the company froze the equivalent of more than $1.5 billion in currency related to "a potential Binance exchange hack."
The price of bitcoin dropped 3.2% Thursday evening to under $79,000.
Binance was founded in 2017 by Changpeng Zhao, who in 2023 pleaded guilty to a felony related to his failure to prevent money laundering on the platform and stepped down as CEO. President Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025.
Technology
As crypto and prediction markets expand, their regulator shrinks
Zhao posted on X on Thursday that "User funds are safe!" but added that the incident "does look like a hack on Binance." He added that while he doesn't manage Binance anymore, "as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."
Zhao was released from prison last year after being sentenced for violating the Bank Secrecy Act. He was the first person ever sentenced to prison time for violations of that law, which requires U.S. financial institutions to know who their customers are, to monitor transactions and to file reports of suspicious activity. Prosecutors said no one had ever violated the regulations to the extent Zhao did. Zhao and Binance have been key supporters of some of the Trump family's crypto enterprises.

You're reading a newsletter from  The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter.  Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.
A TILE GAME is giving a boost to Chinese factories. Our very own Jennifer Pak reported that Chinese manufacturers have not had the easiest few years with U.S. tariffs and the war in Iran pushing up costs. Well, the aged game of Mahjong is giving them a surprising boost. That's because it's having a moment in the U.S. and some entrepreneurial citizens in China are enjoying the benefits. Mahjong sets can sell for like $300-$400 in the States … and want to know how much they cost to make? ~$30. One businessman said he used to make the game primarily for Chinese consumers. Now, every set is exported to the U.S.
People playing the centuries-old game Mahjong in San Francisco, California.

Coming up:
The risks to Anthropic's (and AI's) business
Why we're saying 'buyout' and not 'layoff'
How young people are doing with AI summaries
New's We're Watching
The two most interesting risks to Anthropic - U.S. Securities & Exchange Commission
What to Know: Anthropic gave the world 94 pages of risks to its business (slash the entire AI economy) in its IPO prospectus aka the S-1. It wouldn't be Anthropic if they didn't discuss the "existential risks" to humanity and society several times. And isn't that an important risk to disclose? Another that stood out: the AI boom has a glaring point of failure. The majority of advanced semiconductor manufacturing is concentrated in one place, Taiwan, and if anything were to happen there, it could disrupt the entire AI economy. Think earthquake, Chinese military action, blockades. But I want to focus on a different risk, because it is FASCINATING!
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has persistently raised the safety concerns of AI.
Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images North America
hide caption
Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images North America
Committing to the past at a premium: Anthropic is worried about aging out of the tech that's powering its AI, while paying the same prices. What does that mean?! AI companies have to lock into pricey contracts for all sorts of softwares, hardware, data center, and squadrons of GPUs. But technology is advancing quickly right now. New GPUs, for example, could come along that can do the same amount of work for way less money. Then Anthropic is stuck like CHUMPS in a contract paying a premium for old hardware, while some competitors may be doing more for less.
Why buyouts and not layoffs? - The Wall Street Journal
What To Know: Microsoft offered buyouts to 60,000 employees, roughly a quarter of its staff this week. And doesn't that sound better than "Microsoft laid off 60,000 employees this week"?? Skydance ALSO offered a buyout to employees on Monday, though it's not clear how many would be eligible. And here at NPR, we've been a fan of the term buyout too. So what's the real difference in offering a buyout versus just laying off staffers?
The difference: Morale? Morale. There's something about a "mega-layoff" that doesn't inspire worker confidence. A "buyout" not so much. Really? Ok, I guess. The WSJ reported the focus in C-suite land is on the ratio of employees to AI agents inside companies. Companies have to find ways to pay for the ever-increasing costs of AI … and you know … actual human workers expect to be paid.
Andy Challenger, Chief Revenue Officer of Challenger, Gray & Christmas, a consulting firm, told the Journal that it can help staffers emotionally by making it a little easier to let go. It also tends to motivate older staffers to retire a little bit early, which may be the company's goal.
Today's Indicator
There are more bots than humans online. Here's what that means
If you HAVEN'T listened: I never thought I'd yearn for the days when the internet felt wholesome. Where you could go to blogs and random sites and make friends across the world. Well, more than half of internet traffic now comes from non-humans, aka bots. They're pouring into the digital veins of the World Wide Web, ignoring a lot of ads, generating all kinds of comments, nonsense and what have you. One interesting takeaway: this shift from human-to-bot traffic changes the business model of the internet. If humans let bots do their shopping for them, then ads suddenly become less useful. And if ads don't pay out for websites, then who pays for them?

What's behind scary high candy prices this Halloween Prices for candy, the most popular Halloween purchase, and gum have risen 7.7% in one year and are up more than 18% in two years, according to the latest federal data.
Food
Candy prices got you scared stiff? What to know about the cost of Halloween this year
October 30, 20265:00 AM ET
Heard on All Things Considered
By
Joe Hernandez
Halloween prices & spending
Listen
5:03
5:03
Transcript
Download
Embed
<iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6018566/nx-s1-9984398" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Transcript
Halloween candy is displayed for sale at a Weis Markets grocery store, Thursday, Oct. 22, in Dundalk, Md.
Stephanie Scarbrough/AP
hide caption
Stephanie Scarbrough/AP
For people stocking up on candy this Halloween, it's a spooky season in the grocery store — and not in a fun way.
Prices for candy, the most popular Halloween purchase, and gum have risen 7.7% in one year and are up more than 18% in two years, according to the latest federal data. That's higher than the average rate of food inflation during that time.
Cost of Living
Boo to spooky chocolate prices! It's the year of chewy, fruity Halloween treats
One major culprit: chocolate. Drought and heavy rains in places like West Africa have hurt cocoa harvests in recent seasons and pushed up prices worldwide.
Global cocoa production is now rebounding, but that isn't much help to consumers preparing to hand out candy to peckish trick-or-treaters this weekend, according to David Branch, sector manager with the Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute.
"The candy on the shelves right now — chocolate candy — that cocoa was purchased in 2025," he said. And last year's cocoa prices were high.
Still, rising consumer prices aren't expected to scare people away from celebrating the holiday, with the National Retail Federation estimating consumers will spend $13.5 billion on Halloween this year. That's a 3% annual increase and sets a record: $115 per person, which is 55 cents more than last year.
Hair-raising cocoa prices are moderating
There was a surplus in the global supply of beans earlier this year, and cocoa prices have come down from their recent highs..
NPR's Climate Solutions Week
Scientists tap the power of fermentation to create chocolate without cocoa beans
Yet Branch said consumer chocolate prices are "sticky," meaning they won't fall even when cocoa prices do because of the lag time in production. Manufacturers are also dealing with higher prices on other ingredients like sugar, pricier fuel costs due to the war in Iran and costlier imports subject to U.S. tariffs.
Enna Grazier, who owns the New Hampshire small-batch chocolate company Enna Chocolate, said she is facing a slew of higher costs, including a 50% tariff on some of the holiday packaging and ingredients she planned to purchase from Canadian suppliers.
"I've had to look elsewhere or get creative with some of my packaging needs for this holiday season, and that's super frustrating," Grazier said. "It's meant that I can't plan as far out, or the plans that I did make were disrupted and we've had to pivot and change."
Some candy makers have ushered in a flavor shift in recent years. Companies are offering more gummy and sour candy, and launching products that don't use pricier chocolate, such as KitKat's marshmallow-flavored Witch's Brew and Reese's White Ghosts coated in white creme.
Still, consumer demand for chocolate hasn't melted away. According to data from the market research firm Circana, which tracks purchases in U.S. supermarkets, chocolate candy sales have been increasing for several years running. However, shoppers have been buying less chocolate candy over the same period, which means people are paying more for chocolate and getting less of it.
